name: On-Chain Forensics
title: On-Chain Forensics
answer: On-chain forensics is the practice of reconstructing what happened on a public blockchain by reading its transaction record. It covers tracing the movement of coins between wallets, identifying the entities behind addresses, and mapping the contracts and protocols that funds pass through. The work serves compliance teams, exchanges, law enforcement, journalists and, increasingly, ordinary users trying to understand a counterparty. It sits inside crypto markets and decentralised finance because almost every trade, loan and transfer leaves a permanent public trace.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: On-chain forensics is the practice of reconstructing what happened on a public blockchain by reading its transaction record. It covers tracing the movement of coins between wallets, identifying the entities behind addresses, and mapping the contracts and protocols that funds pass through. The work serves compliance teams, exchanges, law enforcement, journalists and, increasingly, ordinary users trying to understand a counterparty. It sits inside crypto markets and decentralised finance because almost every trade, loan and transfer leaves a permanent public trace.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The raw material is the chain itself, plus archives of decoded transaction and event logs from networks such as Bitcoin and Ethereum. Analysts run indexing software that turns blocks into queryable tables, then layer address labels, exchange deposit lists and contract interfaces on top. Graph databases and visualisation tools hold the relationships between addresses, and clustering heuristics group addresses that appear to share a controller. Some vendors add machine learning to score addresses for risk, but the underlying evidence remains the ledger.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical investigation starts from a known address, a transaction hash or a victim report, then walks forward and backward through transfers. Analysts apply heuristics such as common input ownership, change address detection and reuse of deposit addresses to link wallets. They match timing, gas payment patterns and bridge or mixer interactions to follow funds across chains. Findings are written up as a narrative with the supporting transaction hashes, so another analyst can reproduce each step. Where attribution to a real person or business is claimed, it usually rests on off-chain evidence such as exchange records or public statements.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The evidence produced is used in sanctions screening, suspicious activity reports, exchange account freezes and court proceedings, so chain of custody and reproducibility matter. Address labels are proprietary to the firms that build them, which raises questions about how a cluster was formed and whether it can be challenged. Privacy rules differ by jurisdiction, and mixing services and privacy coins deliberately frustrate tracing. Analysts also face the reverse risk, that a confident label is wrong and harms an innocent party. This page describes practice only and is not legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Tracing is shifting from single chains to cross-chain flows, as bridges and rollups move value between networks with different data models. Account abstraction and smart contract wallets complicate the old assumption that one address equals one user. Regulators are pushing for travel rule data to accompany transfers, which gives analysts more off-chain anchors to work with. At the same time, privacy tooling keeps improving, so the field is likely to stay a contest between better attribution and better obfuscation.
